query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Engineering a nanohierarchical near-surface microstructure in the CoCrFeNi alloy through controlled severe plastic deformation and annealing to induce the in situ formation of a protective, adaptive glaze layer during sliding.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional CoCrFeNi alloy with a uniform, coarse-grained microstructure that exhibits higher friction and wear, particularly under high-temperature sliding.
generation.intervention: Apply a post-synthesis processing route involving severe plastic deformation (e.g., cold rolling achieving ~80% thickness reduction) followed by annealing (e.g., at 700 °C for 1 hour) to generate a fine-grained, nanohierarchical near-surface structure.
generation.conditions: Dry sliding wear tests using a temperature-controlled tribometer over a temperature range from RT to 800 °C under moderate loads akin to those used in previous experiments.
generation.structural_mediator: Development of a nanocoupled grain structure and nanoprecipitates that, upon frictional heating, evolve into a continuous nanocrystalline glaze layer with gradient properties that provide both enhanced hardness and adaptive lubrication.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures, the refined nanostructure improves hardness and reduces plastic deformation, thereby lowering friction. At higher temperatures, the engineered microstructure facilitates a controlled oxidation and glaze formation that acts as a lubricious barrier, reducing metal-to-metal contact and wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: A more consistent, lower friction coefficient and a significantly reduced wear rate across the full temperature range, with marked improvement in high-temperature performance when compared to the untreated CoCrFeNi alloy.
generation.baseline: The untreated CoCrFeNi alloy possessing a coarse, homogeneous microstructure that does not support the formation of an adaptive glaze layer.
generation.boundary: Tribological tests conducted in air under dry sliding conditions with controlled temperatures from RT to 800 °C and normal loads similar to those in prior studies.
generation.uncertainty: The reproducibility of the nanohierarchical microstructure and its stability against grain coarsening at high temperatures depend on precise control of processing parameters; these factors require systematic standardization and further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of samples: one with the engineered nanohierarchical near-surface layer (via severe plastic deformation and annealing) and one with the conventional microstructure. Test both sets in identical sliding wear experiments at RT, 400 °C, and 800 °C.
measurements: Real-time friction coefficient measurements during sliding
Wear rate determination using mass loss and 3D profilometry
Microstructural characterization (EBSD/TEM/SEM) before and after sliding to confirm the presence and persistence of the nanohierarchical structure and glaze layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the engineered samples do not display a clearly lower friction coefficient and reduced wear rate—particularly at high temperatures—or if the expected nanohierarchical structure and glaze layer are absent after testing, the hypothesis must be rejected.

cited_evidence.kind: web:Physical, mechanical, and tribological property measurements
cited_evidence.text: The density of the CCAs was determined by a true density analyzer (AccuPyc-1330). The specific heat and thermal conductivity of the CCAs at RT were determined by a laser thermal conductivity testing instrument (S/N:257-1-316, Germany). High-temperature Vickers hardness tests were performed on an HTV-PHS30 hardness tester (Archimedes Industry Technology Co., UK) under a load of 5 N for 10 s. The sample size of the hardness test was 3 × 10 × 10 mm. The nanoindentation tests were performed on the Anton-Paar NHT3 TriboIndenter system with a Berkovich indenter at RT, with a loading rate of 0.1 mN/s and a peak load of 3.0 mN. A commercial ball-on-disc tribometer (HT-1000, Zhongke-Kaihua Co. Ltd) was used to evaluate the wear evolution of the tested CCAs in the temperature range from RT to 800 °C. The sample size for wear test was Ø 20 × 4 mm (roughness of Ra < 0.02 μm). Si3N4 balls (Ø 6 mm, Vickers hardness of ~15 GPa) were selected as counter materials. Wear tests were conducted at a normal load of 5 N, a sliding speed of 0.2 m/s, and a sliding distance of 360 m. The cross-section profiles and wear volume of the worn tracks were measured by a 3D-optical profilometer (MicroXAM-800). Wear

Both sliding speed and normal load will affect the friction and wear behavior of the different grain size CoCrFeMnNi HEAs. Increasing the sliding speed will increase the friction coefficient and specific wear rate of the alloy. Thus, increase the normal load, reduce the friction coefficient, and decrease the specific wear rate of the alloy. This is because the oxide layer formed on the worn surface under high load plays a role in lubrication and reduces the friction coefficient and specific wear rate.
